name: Catherine the Great
summary: Catherine II was an enlightened absolutist who defended autocracy as suited to Russia's size while drawing on Montesquieu and Beccaria for limits on torture, a preference for toleration and equality under law. In practice she entrenched noble privilege and serfdom, subordinated the Church to the state, crushed the Pugachev rising and expanded the empire through Crimea and the Polish partitions. After 1789 she turned against revolutionary ideas and tightened censorship.

notes:
Rules 7, later pass (earlier passes 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-26; this pass brings the audit up to rules 7). Positions follow the Nakaz (Grand Instruction, 1767, full text from archive.org), the 1763 settlement manifesto, her letters (CatCor), and her recorded acts as reported in Simon Dixon's biography (chapters 1, 5-11 in the local library, read by theme). Under record over words, where a recorded act exists the answer rests on it alone: the Nakaz is cited only where she has no act on the statement. Biography chapters are tier 3 (medium at most); every answer once rated high on a biography was lowered, except the 1763 manifesto and the Orlov instruction, which are her own official acts.
Changes in this pass, each with a reviewHistory entry: Wikipedia-only answers were re-sourced to the biography (political-violence-never, conscription, national-self-determination, annexed-territory-occupation, defensive-wars-only, territorial-expansion, clerical-rule, head-commands-forces, subordinate-church-to-state) or nulled (humanitarian-intervention, majority-settlement, no-religion-state-schools); answers that mixed acts and words were redone from the acts (property-fundamental now 0 low: confirmed noble estates against seized monastic land; bound-labor, equal-moral-worth, death-penalty, abolish-hereditary-privilege, party-controls-media) or nulled where no act in the library settles them (widespread-small-property, suppress-opposition, capital-controls). New: torture-always-illegal (0, low: her coup-era torture of Guards against her 1767 and 1775 restraint; the Nakaz art. 123 calling torture contrary to nature is words and is set aside under record over words).
Searched by theme: government and law (Nakaz on monarchy, courts, torture, capital punishment, serfdom), economy (trade, monopoly, welfare, manufacturing, inheritance), religion (toleration, church lands, orthodoxy), world (Turkey, Poland, Crimea, alliances with Austria), liberty (censorship, presses, Radishchev). Left null: the many modern statements with no counterpart in her record (economy and society statements on wages, unions, same-sex marriage and the like), and everything the library holds no primary text for: see notFound.

Second-round checks (integrator): suppress-opposition and widespread-small-property were redone from the biography (Radishchev and Novikov in Dixon chapters 11-12; serf grants in chapters 10 and 12). The other four nulls were grepped across all biography chapters in the library and kept null: humanitarian-intervention (searched 'dissident', 'dissenters', 'Orthodox minority', 'Greek Project': the text covers the Greek project and Poland as territorial and strategic aims, with no act or statement that settles military intervention for human rights); majority-settlement (searched 'settlers', 'Tatar', Crimea: only the 1760s New Russia colonists, not a majority-settlement policy in minority regions); no-religion-state-schools (searched 'Smolny', 'Commission of National Schools', 'Statute of National Education': the 1782-86 school system and its civic textbook are described without saying whether religion was taught); capital-controls (searched 'assignat', 'banknote', 'paper money', 'specie': no act on cross-border capital movement).
